from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite: The Projection Intuition", ["Dot product measures vector alignment.", "Vectors project as shadows.", "Projection length is the dot product."])
        
        # Define vectors
        v = Vector([1.5, 1.0], color=WHITE)
        b = Vector([2.0, 0], color=BLUE) # Projection subspace
        
        # Calculate projection
        # dot(v, b) / dot(b, b) * b
        dot_vb = v.get_end()[0] * b.get_end()[0] + v.get_end()[1] * b.get_end()[1]
        dot_bb = b.get_end()[0]**2 + b.get_end()[1]**2
        scalar = dot_vb / dot_bb
        p_end = scalar * b.get_end()
        p = Vector(p_end, color="#FFD700") # Projection vector
        
        ortho_comp = Vector(v.get_end() - p.get_end(), color="#FF6347").shift(p.get_end())
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(Create(v), Create(b))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFD700")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(Create(p), Create(ortho_comp))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFD700")
        
        # Highlight right angle
        angle = RightAngle(Line(ORIGIN, p.get_end()), Line(p.get_end(), v.get_end()), length=0.2)
        self.play(Create(angle))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(FadeOut(ortho_comp), FadeOut(angle))
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FFD700")
        self.wait(2)

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["A vector as a linear machine.", "Covectors output scalar scores.", "Dot product powers this mechanism."]
        self.setup_layout("Defining Duality: The Linear Functional", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Display linear functional f(x) = c^T x in #FFFFFF
        formula = MathTex(r"f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{c}^T \mathbf{x}", color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(formula, "B3", scale_factor=1.2)
        self.play(Write(formula))
        self.lecture[0].set_color(ORANGE)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Draw a scalar mapping as a line segment in #00CED1
        scalar_line = Line(start=np.array([-1, 0, 0]), end=np.array([1, 0, 0]), color="#00CED1")
        self.place_at_grid(scalar_line, "D3", scale_factor=1.0)
        scalar_label = Text("Scalar Output", font_size=18, color="#00CED1")
        self.place_at_grid(scalar_label, "E3", scale_factor=0.8)
        self.play(Create(scalar_line), Write(scalar_label))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#00CED1")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Animate input vector x being transformed to scalar f(x)
        vector_x = Arrow(start=ORIGIN, end=UP*1.5, color=YELLOW)
        self.place_at_grid(vector_x, "C2", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        dot = Dot(color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(dot, "D3", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        self.play(GrowArrow(vector_x))
        self.play(vector_x.animate.move_to(self.grid["D3"]), run_time=1.5)
        self.play(FadeOut(vector_x), FadeIn(dot))
        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        self.wait(2)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["Covectors define parallel level lines.", "Dot product counts crossed lines.", "It measures change across planes."]
        self.setup_layout("Visualizing Duality via Level Sets", lecture_lines)
        
        # Grid visualizer: Create parallel lines (level sets)
        lines = VGroup()
        for i in range(-3, 4):
            line = Line(start=[-2, 0.5*i, 0], end=[2, 0.5*i, 0], color="#ADFF2F", stroke_width=2)
            lines.add(line)
        lines.rotate(PI/4)
        self.place_in_area(lines, "B2", "E5", scale_factor=0.6)
        
        # Define the Normal Vector
        normal_vec = Vector(direction=[0.5, 0.5, 0], color="#FFFF00")
        self.place_at_grid(normal_vec, "C3")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(lines), self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#ADFF2F"))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        highlight_line = lines[3].copy().set_stroke(color="#FF4500", width=4)
        self.add(highlight_line)
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#FF4500"))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(GrowArrow(normal_vec), self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#FFFF00"))
        self.wait(1)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Synthesis: Why Duality Matters", [
            "Points and rules are dual.", 
            "This symmetry defines physical laws.", 
            "Duality enables robust machine learning."
        ])
        
        # Define objects
        primal_circle = Circle(radius=0.8, color=BLUE)
        dual_line = Line(start=[-1, 0.5, 0], end=[1, -0.5, 0], color=YELLOW)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        self.place_at_grid(primal_circle, 'B3', 0.8)
        self.play(Create(primal_circle))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.place_at_grid(dual_line, 'D3', 1.0)
        self.play(Create(dual_line))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(GREEN))
        dot_opt = Dot(color=GREEN).move_to(self.grid['C3'])
        self.play(FadeIn(dot_opt))
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: Dot Products and Duality: The Geometry of Measurement

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Projection Intuition
sections.content: Briefly define the dot product (a · b = |a||b|cosθ) as a measure of how much two vectors 'align.' Visualize vector 'a' casting a shadow onto vector 'b'.
sections.example: A flashlight shining on a tilted mirror; the intensity of the light hitting the surface depends on the angle of incidence.

sections.title: Defining Duality: The Linear Functional
sections.content: Introduce a vector not as an arrow, but as a 'machine.' A dual vector (covector) acts on a standard vector to output a scalar. Show the dot product as the mechanism of this machine.
sections.example: Imagine a 'filter' mask. When you pass a vector through the mask (dot product), it outputs a number (a score) representing the vector's alignment with the mask's orientation.

sections.title: Visualizing Duality via Level Sets
sections.content: Explain that a fixed covector w(v) = c defines a set of parallel lines (or hyperplanes) in 2D space. The dot product measures how many of these lines a vector crosses.
sections.example: A hiker walking across a topographical map. The covector is the 'slope direction,' and the dot product tells you how much elevation you gain.

sections.title: Synthesis: Why Duality Matters
sections.content: Conclude that dot products allow us to swap between 'points' (vectors) and 'rules' (dual vectors). This symmetry is foundational for physics (work/energy) and machine learning (SVMs).
sections.example: A 'Robot Sentry': The sentry defines a line (dual vector); any intruder (vector) that crosses the threshold (dot product > 0) triggers an alarm.
